Ulm stool (Ulmer Hocker), 1954

The school’s multipurpose stool by Max Bill, Hans Gugelot, and Paul Hildinger: three spruce boards joined at the corners, with a beech rod between the sides.

Source
Museum Angewandte Kunst, Frankfurt, inventory 17619

Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The museum credits Max Bill, Hans Gugelot, Paul Hildinger, and the Hochschule für Gestaltung Ulm with the design, dates it 1954, places production in Ulm, and gives spruce seat and side panels with a beech dowel and beech trim on the bottom edges. Museum Angewandte Kunst 17619.

The museum says that a small building budget led Gugelot and Bill to keep the furniture simple. The stool “consists of three spruce boards, which are joined together by a finger joint”, and the dowel can be used as a handle. It served as a seat, a book carrier, a low table, a pedestal, or, in a row, a shelf. In 1960 it cost 11 Deutschmarks. Museum Angewandte Kunst.

Observed

  • The stool is an upside-down U of three flat, light spruce boards with straight grain and knots.
  • Finger joints show as a row of small rectangles at both top corners.
  • A round beech rod joins the two sides near the bottom.
  • Thin strips of a slightly different wood edge the bottoms of the sides.
  • There is no finish color, hardware, or ornament.

Why it belongs

The stool is the Ulm method in its most basic form: the fewest parts, visible joints, and a form open to several uses. It shares the structure of the style, not its grey palette.

Borrow

Make the joint the only detail, and repeat it evenly.
